title: Embedded Deployment Evidence and Customer Storyline
author: Avery Chen
content:
Overview:
This document is a field-ready sales enablement brief targeted at engineering and product buyers evaluating embedded or private-deployment inference with Redwood. It combines narrative evidence (a concise customer success storyline), positioning and competitive differentiation for embedded use cases, a slide-by-slide pitch outline for customer meetings, blunt pricing guidance for pilot and POC stages, and a focused security FAQ for technical stakeholders.

Intended audience and use cases:
- Primary audience: Platform/infra engineers, ML engineering leads, CTOs responsible for inference deployments.
- Typical triggers: Regulatory requirement for data residency, offline/air-gapped inference needs, latency or throughput constraints necessitating dedicated GPU pools, or partnership embeds where vendor-hosted inference is not acceptable.

Executive value propositions (short):
- Predictable unit economics at scale: Dedicated pools + batching and KV-caching to reduce token cost by 30–60% vs naive single-request serving.
- Identical developer surface: Same API and rollout controls on Redwood Private as the hosted API—minimal integration friction for product teams.
- Compliance-first packaging: Customer-managed control plane, KMS/HSM integrations, and audit trails designed for SOC2/ISO scope.
- Graceful degradation and fallback: Automated local model variants and cloud fallback routing to keep user-facing features resilient.

Positioning vs common competitive patterns (concise):
- Compared to managed-host providers: Redwood provides a path to run inference in customer VPCs or on-prem with consistent SDK semantics—customers keep control while preserving developer velocity.
- Compared to open-source self-hosting: We offer a hardened runtime, production-grade batching/caching, and an operational way to manage upgrades, rollouts, and fallbacks—reducing ops burden by ~60% in typical TCO analysis.
- Compared to specialized edge vendors: Redwood balances edge-friendly footprints with a full-featured control plane (observability, cost attribution, token-level tracing) so product teams don’t trade observability for locality.

Competitive brief (talking points to highlight differentiators):
- Performance engineering: benchmarked 95th-percentile latency targets, per-model perf profile, and auto-selected kernels for quantized models. State which profiles were validated during the pilot.
- Economic controls: per-route batching & cache policies, quantization recipes, and reserved capacity options to lock unit cost.
- Operational SRE story: deterministic rollouts, canary + automatic fallback to lower-cost variants, and full tracing hooks.
- Compliance & packaging: VPC deployment with customer KMS, audit logs exported to customer SIEM, and optional on-prem distribution for air-gapped customers.

Slide-by-slide pitch outline (20–25 minute meeting):
1) Title & ask: One‑line outcome (e.g., "Pilot to validate sub-50ms inference in-region with full auditability"). Ask: 6–8 week pilot with data-residency clause.
2) Problem statement: Current latency/cost/visibility gaps. 2–3 metrics pulled from discovery.
3) Redwood value snapshot: short bullets with concrete numbers (latency improvement, unit-cost delta, rollback guarantees).
4) Architecture options: hosted vs dedicated vs private (diagram in-slide; call out network boundaries).
5) Integration path: SDK + routing config + rollout steps (3-step integration).
6) Pilot scope & success criteria: sample SLOs and evaluation prompts.
7) Pricing and contract overview (pilot vs production).
8) Security & compliance highlights: KMS, logging, attestation.
9) Customer story (two-slide mini case study).
10) Next steps & mutual action plan.

Pilot pricing guidance (practical rules of thumb):
- Objective: remove friction in procurement while exposing realistic unit economics for production.
- Pilot baseline (6 weeks, single-region private deployment):
  - Setup fee: $10k (engineering onboarding, private control plane, initial model profile).
  - Monthly pilot run charge: $8k for reserved capacity sized for ~200 concurrent sessions or ~5M tokens/mo (includes limited support and 7x12 monitoring).
  - Option to add burst capacity at usage-based rates if customer needs spike.
- Alternative lightweight lab pilot: hosted sandbox (no private deployment) with $0 setup, limited to 1M tokens and 2-week duration—good for rapid product validation.
- Production conversion: pilots typically convert to a Reserved Capacity contract. Typical ask: 12–18 month commit; example tiers: small (2 GPUs reserved), medium (8 GPUs), large (32 GPUs) with discounts starting at 30% on list for longer commitments.
- Pricing caveats and negotiation levers: commit duration, model quantization profile (smaller models -> lower cost), and observability retention window. For enterprise deals, include an optional success-based credit tied to meeting initial SLOs.

Closing checklist for pilots (for AE/SE team):
1) Define three measurable pilot success criteria (latency p95, token cost delta, and functional accuracy on eval set).
2) Confirm network & compliance pre-requisites (VPC peering, firewall rules, KMS onboarding).
3) Scope model(s) and prompt sets; capture baseline metrics from customer.
4) Define rollback & escalation path; assign on-call SRE for pilot window.
5) Agree on observed data to share during weekly reviews (latency histograms, token counts, error rates).

Customer story: Compact case study (two pages, single narrative):
- Customer: FinTech payments platform ("AcmePay"), 150M monthly transactions, strong regulatory constraints across EU and US.
- Challenge: In-app transaction summarization and fraud-signal enrichment needed sub-100ms in-region inference, with full audit trail and no cross-border PII transfer.
- Pilot approach: 8-week Private deployment in EU region, reserved capacity sized for peak hours, limited KV-prefix caching for repeated user prompts, and local KMS integration for key management.
- Outcomes: p95 latency improved from 290ms (cloud-hosted baseline) to 72ms; per-token cost down 38% through batching and quantization profile; compliance audit checklist passed for data residency controls.
- Key quotes: "We hit our latency goals without sacrificing auditability—integration took two sprints and the Redwood team owned the rollout operations."

Security FAQ (for prospect technical reviewers):
Q: How is data encrypted in transit and at rest in Private deployments?
A: TLS 1.2+ for all control and data plane traffic; at rest we use customer-managed KMS (AES-256) where the control plane stores only encrypted metadata. For on-prem packages, volumes are expected to use standard FDE and we support HSM attestations.

Q: What access controls and RBAC can we apply?
A: RBAC mirrors the console model: token-scoped roles, route-level scopes, and audit log exports. For Private, auth integrates with your IdP (SAML/OIDC) and we support SCIM for user lifecycle.

Q: Do you offer a full attestation or penetration test report?
A: Yes—Redwood provides SOC2 Type II reports on request for hosted services and a penetration test summary for the Private product. Enterprise customers can request on-site pen-tests as part of the engagement.

Q: How do you prevent model or prompt leakage across tenants?
A: Private deployments run isolated runtime instances per customer. KV caches and model artifacts are namespaced. For multi-tenant Dedicated offerings, we enforce strict memory isolation between tenant containers and restrict cross-tenant routing policies.

Q: What about secure model updates and rollback safety?
A: Model artifacts are signed and versioned. Rollouts use canary windows with automatic traffic diversion to signed fallback variants if regressions are detected per configured eval prompt sets.

Q: How much telemetry is sent back to Redwood?
A: For Private installs telemetry can be disabled. The default setup collects health metrics and anonymized runtime diagnostics; audit logs and token-level traces are exported to the customer SIEM. All telemetry adheres to the agreed confidentiality settings in the contract.

Technical appendix (short examples):
- Integration snippet (pseudo-CLI to install private control plane):
  1) Customer prepares VPC and KMS: set up subnet A, egress rules, and KMS key ARN.
  2) Installer: redwood-install --control-plane-endpoint https://cp.company.example --kms-arn arn:aws:kms:eu-west-1:123456:key/abcd1234 --region eu-west-1
  3) After install, create route and model profile:
     POST /api/v1/routes {"name":"acme-pay-summarize","model":"gptx-16k-q4","slo_p95_ms":100} (Example payload shown in onboarding runbook).

- Sample SLOs to propose in agreement:
  - Availability: 99.9% per calendar month for pilot support; 99.95% for production reserved tiers.
  - Latency: p95 <= target (negotiated per-feature).
  - Error rate: <0.5% API errors excluding timeouts.

Objection handling quick scripts (SE cheats):
- "We can self-host with open-source stacks": Acknowledge viability, then pivot: "great—Redwood reduces ops effort by providing kernel selection, perf profiles, and an observability plane; we typically cut TTM and ops costs by more than half versus homegrown approaches" and show pilot metrics.
- "We are worried about vendor lock-in": Emphasize API compatibility and clear export paths for artifacts and logs; hand over model and prompt artifacts at contract close.
- "We need full air-gap": Confirm on-prem installer and offline deployment options; outline extra support and acceptance testing required.

Operational ownership and roles (during pilot):
- Redwood: pilot lead (SE), deployment SRE, solution architect, and a named security reviewer.
- Customer: platform owner, network engineer, and ML lead for evaluation criteria.

Next steps (mutual action plan template):
1) Kickoff: schedule within 5 business days of LOI.
2) Network & compliance checklist completion: 7 days.
3) Private control plane install & basic smoke tests: 10 business days.
4) Integration + baseline collection: 2 weeks.
5) Weekly review syncs + final evaluation: last 2 weeks of pilot.
